title: Scaling Laws
oneLineScope: Loss as a smooth power law in parameters, data, and compute — the empirical regularity (Kaplan et al. 2020) that made scale predictable.
prose:
Where we are. We arrived here from two directions. The autoregressive-lm node gave us the training objective — predict the next token, and drive down the cross-entropy loss of doing so — and the data-and-compute node described the growing appetite for text and hardware that training such models demands. That appetite raises an uncomfortable question: is feeding it worth it? If you double the model, double the data, double the spend, do you get a proportionate return, or are you pouring money into a bucket that is nearly full? This node answers that question with a measurement.

The gist. Around 2020, Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI trained language models across a wide range of sizes and dataset sizes and plotted how well each one did against how big it was. The striking result is that the test loss falls as a smooth, predictable power law in three quantities — the model’s size, the amount of training data, and the total compute — and it does so over orders of magnitude of scale, with no knee or plateau anywhere in the measured range. In words a statistician will recognize instantly: plot the loss against scale on log-log axes and you get a straight line.

Why it matters. A straight line you can extrapolate turns scaling from a gamble into a forecast. Before this, “make it bigger” was a hunch; afterward, you could fit the curve on small, cheap runs and read off, in advance, the loss a hundred-times-larger run would reach. That single fact is the economic argument that justified spending tens of millions of dollars on a single training run — and so it is the hinge between the architecture half of this story and the era of deliberately enormous models that follows.

The intuition, in your own language

Strip away the deep-learning vocabulary and this is a phenomenon you have characterized many times. We have a system with a tunable resource — call it \(x\), the scale — and a performance measure that improves as we add resource but with diminishing returns. The empirical claim is that the returns diminish in the most orderly way possible: the loss is proportional to \(x^{-\alpha}\) for some positive exponent \(\alpha\). That is a power law, the same object that shows up in critical phenomena, in Zipf’s law over word frequencies (a curve this reader knows from linguistics), and in countless natural systems. Its signature is scale-invariance: every tenfold increase in the resource buys the same additive drop in \(\log\)-loss, whether you are going from a million parameters to ten million or from a billion to ten billion.

Make it concrete. Suppose a small model reaches a loss of, say, four nats per token, and you find that multiplying its size by ten brings the loss down by a fixed step. The power-law claim is that the next tenfold increase brings it down by the same step, and the next, and the next — a metronome, not a wall. The slope of that descent on log-log paper is the exponent \(\alpha\), and the surprising empirical finding is not that the loss improves — everyone expected that — but that the improvement is this regular, this far, with no sign of the bucket filling up inside the window they could afford to probe.

What was measured

The quantity being driven down — the y-axis — is exactly the objective from the autoregressive-lm node: the cross-entropy loss on held-out text, in nats per token. This is the same negative log-likelihood the model is trained to minimize, and it is precisely \(\log\) of perplexity, so a statistician can read it either as an information-theoretic code length or as an effective branching factor. Kaplan et al. varied three inputs, each over a wide range, and watched this loss respond:

  • \(N\) — the number of model parameters, counting only the non-embedding weights (the attention and feed-forward matrices, not the token and position embedding tables). They found that including the embeddings muddies the relationship and that excluding them makes the law cleaner.
  • \(D\) — the dataset size, in tokens.
  • \(C\) — the training compute, in floating-point operations, well approximated by \(C \approx 6 N D\): six FLOPs per parameter per token (two for the forward multiply-add, four for the backward pass). This back-of-envelope identity is what lets you trade parameters against tokens against a dollar budget on a single axis.

The law itself

With the intuition in hand the formalism is almost a transcription. Vary one of the three resources while holding the others non-limiting, and the loss obeys

\[ L(N) \approx \left( \frac{N_c}{N} \right)^{\alpha_N}, \qquad L(D) \approx \left( \frac{D_c}{D} \right)^{\alpha_D}, \qquad L(C) \approx \left( \frac{C_c}{C} \right)^{\alpha_C} . \]

Read each factor as the power law from the intuition, written in a tidy form. Each \(\alpha\) is a positive scaling exponent — the slope of the line on log-log axes, the thing the whole result is about. Each subscripted constant (\(N_c, D_c, C_c\)) is a horizontal offset: it sets where the curve would notionally cross \(L = 1\), one nat. So the form says nothing exotic — \(y \sim x^{-\alpha}\) is a straight line of slope \(-\alpha\) once you take logs of both axes, and that is exactly what the data trace out.

The fitted exponents are small — on the order of \(\alpha_N \approx 0.076\) and \(\alpha_D \approx 0.095\) for the parameter and data laws, with the compute exponent in a similar range. A small exponent means the loss falls slowly: you need roughly an order of magnitude more resource to make a visible dent. But it falls with metronomic regularity, and that regularity, not the speed, is the headline.

It is worth saying plainly where the science is, because the reader will carry this forward. The functional form is the finding; the exponents are fit, not derived. There is no first-principles theory here that hands you \(\alpha_N \approx 0.076\) from the architecture — these are empirical regularities of exactly the kind you have spent a career characterizing, complete with confidence intervals and a domain of validity, not theorems. The remarkable content is not the particular numbers but that a relationship this simple holds this well across so many decades of scale. Treat it as you would any well-fit empirical power law: trust it firmly inside the fitted range, and extrapolate beyond it only with the caution you would apply to any fit pushed past its support.

One refinement keeps the form honest at the limits. A pure power law \(L \sim x^{-\alpha}\) heads to zero as the resource grows without bound, which cannot be right — natural language has a nonzero entropy, so there is an irreducible floor the loss can approach but never cross. Kaplan et al. accommodate this by fitting, when model size and data are jointly varied, a combined surface that adds the two effects and tends to a positive constant rather than to zero: schematically \(L(N, D)\) behaves like an \(N\)-term plus a \(D\)-term plus that floor, so whichever of model size or data is the binding constraint dominates the loss. The clean single-variable power laws above are what you see when one factor is the bottleneck and the others are held generous; the joint fit is what tells you which knob is currently limiting you, and therefore worth turning. For a statistician this is the familiar discipline of writing the saturating term explicitly rather than trusting a log-linear fit out past its support.

What follows from a power law

Three consequences mattered enough to change how models were built. First, loss became predictable: fit the line on small, cheap runs and you can read off, in advance, the loss a far larger run will reach. That is what justified the capital — you were interpolating along a measured curve, not betting blind. Second, performance depends strongly on the scale variables \((N, D, C)\) and only weakly on architectural shape: within reason, how you split a parameter budget between depth (number of layers \(L\)) and width (\(d_{\text{model}}\)) barely moves the loss — total \(N\) is what counts. After a decade of architecture-tinkering, that result was bracing. Third, larger models are more sample-efficient: a bigger model reaches any given loss having seen fewer tokens than a smaller one would need.

That last point flips an old training instinct. The classical move is to train a model to convergence — push it until the loss stops improving on your data. Kaplan et al. argue that under a fixed compute budget this is wasteful: you do better to train a large model and stop it well short of convergence than to grind a small model all the way down. Given a compute budget \(C\), there is an optimal model size \(N\), and the leftover budget goes into tokens; pouring compute into a too-small network past the point of efficient return is the mistake the law warns against.

The correction you must carry: Chinchilla

This is the place to be careful, because the field corrected itself two years later, and you should not leave with Kaplan as the last word on allocation. Kaplan’s own recipe for spending a compute budget leaned heavily toward model size: their analysis suggested that as you scale compute, most of it should go into more parameters and comparatively little into more data. Acting on that, the large models of 2020–2021 were built very big and trained on relatively few tokens.

In 2022 Hoffmann et al. — the Chinchilla paper — redid the compute-optimal analysis more carefully and reached a sharply different allocation: for compute-optimal training, model size and the number of training tokens should scale in roughly equal proportion, about \(1\!:\!1\), as the budget grows. By that accounting the headline models that preceded it were significantly under-trained — too many parameters chasing too little data. Their demonstration was a model (Chinchilla) substantially smaller than a contemporary giant but trained on far more tokens, which nonetheless outperformed it across the board at equal compute. The clean way to hold both papers in mind: Kaplan established that loss is a power law in scale — the foundational, still-standing result — and Chinchilla corrected the recipe for how to divide a fixed budget between \(N\) and \(D\). The straight lines were right; the early advice on which line to walk along was not.

Where it leads

The two power-law facts — that loss falls predictably with scale, and that you should balance \(N\) against \(D\) to fall fastest — together make a clear recommendation: build the largest model the curve and the budget allow. That recommendation leads directly into in-context-learning. Once OpenAI acted on it and trained GPT-3 — a model far larger than anything before it — an unbilled surprise fell out: the model could learn a new task from a handful of examples placed in its prompt, with no weight update at all. The scaling laws are the economic argument that made building such a model worth the expense; the next node is about the capability that emerged when they did.

diagrams.caption: The iconic scaling-law plot: test loss falls as a straight line against compute (and against model size N and dataset size D) on log-log axes; the slope is the power-law exponent.
diagrams.altText: Three small log-log plots side by side. In each, the horizontal axis is log scale and the vertical axis is the test cross-entropy loss on a log scale. The left plot has loss versus training compute C; the middle plot has loss versus model parameters N; the right plot has loss versus dataset size D. In every plot the data form a descending straight line spanning several orders of magnitude, and the line's slope is labeled as the negative power-law exponent (minus alpha). A note reads: straight line on log-log axes means loss is a power law in that quantity.
diagrams.prompt: Structural figure: three small log-log plots arranged left to right, sharing a style. Title above the row: 'Test loss is a power law in each of N, D, C'. Each plot has a horizontal axis labeled as a logarithmic scale and a vertical axis labeled 'test loss L (log scale)'. Left plot: horizontal axis 'training compute C (FLOPs, log)'. Middle plot: horizontal axis 'model size N (params, log)'. Right plot: horizontal axis 'dataset size D (tokens, log)'. In each plot draw a single descending straight line of data points running from upper-left to lower-right, spanning the full width to suggest several orders of magnitude. Label the slope of each line with its exponent: the compute plot 'slope = −alpha_C', the size plot 'slope = −alpha_N', the data plot 'slope = −alpha_D'. Emphasize the straightness of the lines as the central message. Add one margin note with a leader line pointing at a line: 'straight on log-log axes = power law: L is proportional to x to the minus alpha'. Structural diagram: the axes (both log), the descending straight lines, and the slope-equals-exponent labels must be exact. Do not put specific numeric loss values on the axes.

diagrams.caption: More parameters plus more data plus more compute drive the loss down predictably along the curve — with Chinchilla's later correction that model size and tokens should scale together.
diagrams.altText: On the left, three stacked inputs labeled more parameters N, more data D, and more compute C feed into a downhill arrow. The arrow leads to a lower, predictable loss on the right, drawn as a ball rolling down a smooth slope. A separate note at the bottom reads: Chinchilla 2022 correction — for a fixed compute budget, scale model size N and training tokens D together, roughly one to one; earlier large models were under-trained on data.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual illustration. On the left, three stacked labeled inputs: 'more parameters (N)', 'more data (D)', 'more compute (C)'. Arrows from all three converge into a single broad downhill arrow flowing to the right. The downhill arrow leads to a label on the right: 'lower loss — and predictable'. Reinforce the 'predictable' idea by drawing the descent as a smooth downward slope with a ball partway down it, suggesting you can see where it is heading. Below the main flow, set apart in its own boxed note, write the correction: 'Chinchilla (2022): for a fixed compute budget, scale model size N and training tokens D together — roughly 1:1. Earlier large models had too many parameters for too little data (under-trained).' Emphasize the contrast between the main message (scale everything up, loss goes down predictably) and the correction (balance N against D). No equations beyond the simple ratio 1:1; no axes or plots — this is the intuition companion to the log-log plot. Conceptual analogy: vibe over precise labels.

bibliography.citation: Kaplan, J., McCandlish, S., et al. (2020). "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models." arXiv:2001.08361.
bibliography.annotation: The foundational result, and the source of the power-law form this node is built on. §1 (Summary) states the laws and exponents up front; §3 fits L(N), L(D), L(C) individually and jointly; §6 makes the compute-optimal, sample-efficiency, and 'don't train small models to convergence' arguments. Read §6 knowing its allocation recipe was revised by Chinchilla. The C ≈ 6ND derivation is in the appendix.

bibliography.citation: Hoffmann, J., Borgeaud, S., et al. (2022). "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models" (Chinchilla). arXiv:2203.15556.
bibliography.annotation: The crucial correction to Kaplan's allocation, and the second fact to carry forward. §3 derives, by three independent methods that agree, that model size and training tokens should scale roughly equally (≈1:1) for compute-optimal training, implying prior large models were under-trained on data. Read it as the revised recipe for dividing a budget, not a refutation of the power-law form, which it leaves standing.

A serviceable, frequently-updated overview that states the power-law form, lists the Kaplan and Chinchilla exponents side by side, and explains the C ≈ 6ND estimate. Useful for seeing the two papers reconciled in one place; check its citations rather than trusting figures blind.

expansion: Deeper treatment deliberately omitted from the prose, to be expanded strictly from the cited sources: (1) the exact Kaplan exponents and crossover constants with their fitted ranges and the joint loss surface L(N,D) including the finite-size and finite-data correction terms — Kaplan §§3-4; (2) the derivation of C ≈ 6ND from forward/backward FLOP counts — Kaplan appendix; (3) the compute-optimal frontier N_opt(C), D_opt(C) and the precise sense in which early models were under-trained — contrast Kaplan §6 against Hoffmann §3, including why the two analyses disagreed (learning-rate schedule treatment); (4) the three independent estimation methods in Chinchilla and their agreement. Cite each claim to its source section; introduce no numbers absent from the bibliography.
